questions.context:
Unit: Central Immune Organs and Lymph Flow.
Worked-case data: A small skin abrasion introduces material into tissue fluid of the left foot. Trace a plausible route toward immune surveillance and return to blood.
Separate investigation observations:
Origin: Antigen enters interstitial fluid around a skin abrasion.
Transport: Afferent lymph carries antigen-bearing cells from the tissue.
Cell encounter: Mature naive lymphocytes meet presented antigen in organized lymphoid tissue.

criteria.answer: CO2 raises H+ and lowers pH; central chemoreceptors stimulate respiratory centers, increasing breathing rate and depth to expel CO2. Award 0.25 each for CO2/pH, chemoreceptors, respiratory stimulation, and increased rate/depth.
Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary vasoconstriction, redirecting blood to better-ventilated alveoli. Award 0.5 for constriction and 0.5 for redistribution.
Increased CO2/decreased pH, increased temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG. Award one third per distinct factor group.
Water (H2O), carbonic acid (H2CO3), and carbonic anhydrase (CA). Award one third per blank.
Dissolved in plasma; as bicarbonate after CO2 reacts with water; and bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin. Award one third per form.
Kidneys produce erythropoietin (EPO). Award 0.5 for each.
Any four of duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, descending colon, and rectum, as in the source key. Accept appropriate qualification of retroperitoneal portions; 0.25 per distinct correct structure.

The pancreas supplies bicarbonate-rich juice to the duodenum, neutralizing acid and providing an appropriate pH for intestinal enzymes. Award 0.5 for pancreatic bicarbonate and 0.5 for neutralization.
Soft palate and uvula rise to close the nasopharynx; the epiglottis covers the glottis. Award one third per blank.
Incisors; they cut/bite food, so food must be precut or supplied in bite-sized pieces. Award 0.5 for incisors and 0.5 for function/effect.

Bicarbonate-rich mucus protects against acid and enzymes; tight junctions prevent penetration into underlying tissue; rapid epithelial replacement repairs damage. Award up to 1 point proportionally for a coherent barrier explanation including the need to prevent acid/enzymatic injury.
Carbohydrate/protein digestion products enter blood capillaries in villi; most dietary lipids enter lacteals and reach blood via lymph. Award 0.5 for each route.
To prevent pancreatic self-digestion; activated in the duodenum/small intestine. Award 0.5 each.

The primary response produces plasma cells and memory B cells; memory B cells respond to a subsequent encounter with the antigen. Award 0.5 for memory-cell formation and 0.5 for their secondary response.
The heart actively pumps blood; lymph is propelled by skeletal muscle/body movements and breathing, with one-way valves preventing backflow. Award 0.5 for the blood pump and 0.5 for lymph transport.
Superior lobe of the right lung
accepted: Superior lobe of the right lung

criteria.answer: Phosphorus and nitrogen, as it comes from agricultural fertilizers and residential runoff. The nitrogen and phosphorus (especially) can lead to watershed eutrophication, eventually leading to “dead zones”.
Dendritic drainage patterns are the most common drainage pattern.
Anastomose channels are basically braided stream channels, but they don’t divide or reconnect as easily as braided stream channels.
Waterfalls are usually formed when water flowing above harder rock erodes away at softer rock, downcutting it.

Lake Tanganyika was formed as a part of the western branch of the East African Rift, thus making it a rift lake. As how other rift lakes are formed, Lake Tanganyika was most likely formed from the rifting and subsidence of parts of the African plate ~9-12 million years ago.

sediment budget is difficult to calculate because it is difficult to calculate the exact amount of sediment added or subtracted from a certain area and all the sources and sinks of sediment must be taken into account.

The rapidly growing population needed a dam to provide enough water. The construction of a high dam at Aswan tampered with the river’s delicate flow patterns, thus diminishing the seasonal flooding at the bank. The controlled outflow of water from the dam into Lake Nasser meant that it accumulated ~98% of the suspended sediment usually carried downstream. This is not good as agriculture required the rich sediment deposited when the river used to seasonally flood, leading to increased fertilizer use which leads to higher water pollution.
gravel, sand, silt, clay, and salts
Darcy’s law states that the negative of permeability/dynamic viscosity of the fluid multiplied by the pressure drop is equal to the instantaneous flow rate of a fluid.
The “fried egg” formation was formed when workers accidentally snapped off two stalagmites, and tourists at Luray Caverns have eroded the stalagmites into the “fried egg” shape.

Both stalagmites & stalactites are formed when calcite salts precipitates from groundwater on cave walls; stalagmites precipitate from the floor up, while stalactites precipitate from the roof of the cave and up, almost like icicles.
Yes, as after the volcano erupts and the depression is formed, the lake forms and clay called hectorite can accumulate.
The water flows back into watersheds, is absorbed into the ground as groundwater, and erodes Earth’s surfaces as it flows back into watersheds.

Karst formations are formed when soft, water-soluble bedrock such as limestone, dolomite, gypsum, & marble gets dissolved by running water, forming distinct features such as sinkholes, springs, and streams.
Sinkholes can be from either the erosion or removal of soluble bedrock (i.e. limestone) from running water, collapse of a cave roof, lowering of a water table, or overwithdrawal of groundwater.

The photo shows a tidal marsh. Tidal marshes form in areas that are sheltered from waves, and they drain and flood based off the tidal pattern of the adjacent watershed (i.e. rivers, estuaries, oceans). They are found along rivers, coasts, or seas, and can be freshwater or saline.

Groundwater is naturally filtered as it passes through layers of material and porous soil--groundwater is generally cleaner than surface water since surface water has chemicals, pollutants, organisms, and other materials that aren’t filtered out like groundwater. Groundwater is usually safe to drink unlike surface water.
No (generally), as the particles of silt are larger than clay, thus meaning silt has more pore space than clay, on average.

The salt levels in seawater is way too high for the human body as human kidneys cannot get rid of the excess salt, plus seawater is dehydrating; there is no overarching issued “safe” level of dissolved salt in drinking water, USGS says to not exceed levels above 500 mg/L to avoid the salty taste.
Seasonal lakes are named ephemeral lakes since “ephemeral” means “lasting temporarily”, and seasonal lakes only hold water for short periods, thus ephemeral describes seasonal lakes well.
A black-and-white Secchi disk is generally used to measure freshwater turbidity.
Xeriscaping, especially with native plants, reduces the amount of fertilizers and pesticides that get washed up into local watersheds, and, most importantly, conserves water.

Asian Carp outcompetes native animals, disrupting the ecosystem. Plus, they can survive in lower quality water, killing off sensitive indicator organisms. Asian Carp also jump out of water to evade threats, which can injure people paddling in the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Lastly, they cost the Mississippi River area’s fishing industry $7 billion annually by outcompeting native fish (those that are usually caught and sold).

The Chesapeake Bay supplies a lot of seafood and recreational spots that many states rely on for economy, and the wetlands and watersheds shelter diverse communities of life and soften coastal storms.

The likelihood of droughts occurring are predicted by monitoring rainfall, river flow, and soil moisture. The water table changes, as the water table and aquifers rely on rainfall to replenish the levels of the water. The height of the water table drops as the rate water is pumped from the ground exceeds the rate the water can be replenished, thus the ground subsides and sinks.
An aquifer is a layer of underground permeable rock that holds groundwater.

Groundwater drilling, or groundwater extraction causes land subsidence, lack of surface water, and lowered water quality in aquifers. If there is too much extraction of groundwater, the water table lowers thus leading to wells not being able to reach groundwater; watersheds like rivers that connect to groundwater will also have the water supply diminished. Thus, no, groundwater extraction is not ethical for the environment.

Land subsidence is sometimes due to the lowering of the water table or excess pumping of groundwater; the sediments that hold up the land with water now partially lowers due to the loss of groundwater, causing land to drop and changing the topographic gradient. Land subsidence also reduces aquifers’ abilities to store water, most likely changing the water quality and altering underground sediments.

Arsenic gets into drinking water sources either naturally or artificially from industrial waste and agricultural pollution (certain fertilizers contain arsenic). Antimony gets into drinking water often from being dissolved in metal plumbing/fittings.
the unsaturated zone is usually 0-100+ m underground, depending on climate and land type.
The water balance equation is an important part of hydrology as it displays the system of hydrology as a whole using the conservation of mass.
Labels: River, Perched water table, Unsaturated zone, Water table, Aquifer (labeled diagram in the published key; any order accepted).

Deforestation, poorly managed construction sites, winter road sanding, erosion/exposed soil, overgrazing/bad agricultural practice all lead up to excess weathering/erosion of surface sediments. The sediment eventually washes up into rivers and other watersheds, leading to excess sediments in watersheds. Dams also alter the patterns of sediment transport, adding on to the problem.

Excess sediment leads to altered water depth and altered water flow, thus making watersheds more difficult to navigate. Water quality also goes down, such as increased turbidity, TDS (total dissolved solids), and TSS (total suspended solids). The extra sediment also disrupts the balance of watershed ecosystems, harming delicate indicator species and others alike.

Firstly, flow patterns are disrupted, thus affecting habitats as sediment transport patterns change. Adding on, water quality factors such as dissolved oxygen levels and temperature are changed. Cold, oxygen-deprived water is released from the reservoir bottom, affecting water quality. Sediments, logs, gravel, etc. can be trapped in dams, creating pools downstream and burying the riverbeds where fish spawn.

Disrupted flow patterns affect migrating fish and disrupt the fragile ecosystem balance. Dissolved oxygen levels and temperatures are especially affected: surface water annual temperature variation increases while deep water annual temperature variation does the opposite; this is not good for sensitive species. Temperature also affects dissolved oxygen levels, thus leading to algal blooms and lower dissolved oxygen levels. Dams block rivers from migrating fish, disrupting the surrounding ecosystem once again.

1) Excess nutrients (ammonia/ammonium, nitrates, phosphates) and sediments are introduced to a watershed (mainly lakes), whether through human activity (i.e. an overabundance of fertilizer washing into a local lake) or naturally. 2) The introduction of abnormal levels of nutrients lead to algae rapidly blooming. This algal bloom; the water appears murky, covered in “scum” (the algae), and overall disgusting. Often, sediment washes in too, thus continuing the negative feedback loop of more algae growing.
3) Algae blocks sunlight from reaching the bottom of the affected area & uses up a lot of oxygen. 4) Eventually, the water becomes so depleted of oxygen organisms it becomes a “dead zone”.

It is usually part of the water table as the part where water table that naturally meets the surface is considered still a water table but it could be a watershed such as a stream, river, or lake. If we look at it a different way, it is not considered part of a water table as a watershed is a drainage basin where all precipitation drains to an endorheic basin, while a water table is the horizontal depth of the top of the aquifer. Thus, no and yes.
Meanders are formed when water erodes sediment in the outer bank of a stream.
They are mildly common especially in the middle & lower course of a bridge.
Each natural lake is formed when a depression called a lake basin gets filled in with water, or from an existing body of water. The way the lake basin forms varies.

Cirque/tarn lakes, Glacial lakes, Rock hollow lakes, Volcanic lakes, Meteorite lakes, Solution lakes, Fluvial lakes, Oxbow lakes, Landslide lakes, Tectonic lakes, Aeolian lakes, Freshwater lakes, Organic/animal-made lakes, Saline lakes, Barrier lakes, Rift valley lakes, Karst lakes, Wind deflation lakes, Human-made/artificial lakes, Permanent lakes, Temporary lakes (and their respective formation mechanisms as detailed in the key).

Groundwater pumping for oil & gas extraction, groundwater extraction, contamination that seeps into the ground such as dumping toxic waste or landfill/waste disposal or agricultural contaminants, urban & industrial discharges all human activities that affects groundwater

Groundwater pumping contaminates groundwater and alters how water moves between a watershed, aquifer, and groundwater by intercepting groundwater flow that discharges into the surface-water body, or increasing the rate of water movement from the surface-watershed into an aquifer, leading to an aquifer holding too much water that discharges to surface watersheds that exacerbates erosion, altering aquatic life. Groundwater extraction leads to land subsidence and changes in topography; contaminants from things such as landfill waste can seep into the groundwater, again discharging to surrounding soil and watersheds, being toxic to life, decreasing ground- and surface- water quality; urban and industrial discharge might have similar effects to landfill waste.

If the original rock contains aluminum-bearing minerals, then over long periods of laterization, the aluminum accumulates while other components wash away. The end result is a bauxite deposit. (+3)

(+1) Typically on Earth, Hematite is a good indication of water being present, which is why hematite is particularly interesting in the exploration of Mars as a possible indication for life and evidence that water existed on Mars (+2)

What are the 6 different symmetries/systems that can occur in different minerals that can allow twinning? Tiebreaker Triclinic, Monoclinic, Orthrombic, Tetragonal, Hexagonal, Isometric (+0.5 each)

Describe the difference between contact and penetration twinning. Contact twinning occurs when two crystal individuals share a single, planar twin boundary and meet along that flat surface. Penetration twinning involves two intergrown crystals that intersect in a more complex, often interpenetrating geometry with a non-planar twin boundary. (+2)
Identify the following Amazonite (+1), if answer Microcline/orthoclase only give (+0.5)

Microcline and orthoclase have the same composition and different crystal structures, so they illustrate polymorphism. Amazonite is a variety of microcline, not a separate polymorph contrasted with microcline.
Does this mineral exhibit perfect cleavage (Y/N)? Y (+1)

Fill in the blank. This mineral reacts with __ to create __. Silica (+1), Pyroxene (+1).

Describe the concept of fractional crystallization. Which elements are removed early on and which elements remain after a long period of time in this process? Fractional crystallization is the process in which early-formed minerals crystallize from a cooling magma and are removed from the melt as they settle by gravity, causing the remaining liquid to change composition over time. (+1) Early-forming minerals remove Mg, Fe, and Ca, while the melt becomes progressively enriched in Si, Na, and K as crystallization continues. (+1)

What’s the difference between the continuous and discontinuous reaction series? Be as specific as possible and describe when the continuous and discontinuous reaction series converge. Tiebreaker Plagioclase Feldspar begins crystallizing roughly at the same time as pyroxene on the Discontinuous Series. At this temperature, Plagioclase Feldspar is calcium-rich, but it becomes more sodium-rich as temperature decreases. The series is continuous because the mineral is always Plagioclase Feldspar. (+2, +1 for naming the first mineral and change in composition as temperature decreases) The discontinuous series is the process described in question 4) where olivine goes to pyroxene then amphibole to biotite then potassium feldspar as temperature decreases (+1 for describing process). At potassium feldspar, the discontinuous and continuous pathways converge (+1).
Name two subtypes of this mineral and describe briefly how they differ chemically. Fayalite, iron rich (+1) Forsterite, magnesium rich
What two minerals are present in the sample? Malachite and Azurite (+2)
What is the chemical composition of both minerals? Cu2CO3(OH)2 for malachite (+1) Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2 for azurite (+1)
Will this mineral react with acid at low temperatures? What about high temperatures? Malachite will react with acid at low and high temperatures (+1)

How are these two minerals related when they occur together and how can one mineral lead to the formation of the other? The two represent different stages of the same geochemical process: azurite forms under slightly higher CO2 conditions, while malachite forms when CO2 is lower (+1) Azurite is unstable in air and is usually pseudo-morphically replaced by malachite (+1)
These minerals are good indicators of what deposit? Copper deposits (+1)
What’s the hardness of both minerals? Both around 3.5-4 (+1)
What crystal habit does the specimen show? Botroiydal (+1)
Identify the following Mica Schist (+1), only 0.5+ for schist
A: sill. B: dike/dyke. C: laccolith. D: batholith. Award one point for each correct label.

Define what a Xenolith is. A xenolith is a fragment of rock that becomes trapped inside a different rock, most commonly when older rock is torn off and incorporated into magma, which then hardens into an igneous rock, +1 point
You discover a tabular igneous body that is concordant with sedimentary bedding but has baked contacts both above and below. What type of intrusion is it? Tiebreaker +1 Sill

Superposition: younger beds overlie older beds in an undeformed sequence. Original horizontality: sediments are initially deposited approximately horizontally. Lateral continuity: beds originally extend laterally until thinning or reaching a boundary. Cross-cutting: the cutting feature is younger than what it cuts. Award credit for the meaning of each specified principle.

A: greenschist. B: amphibolite. C: blueschist. These are qualitative positions in a supplied schematic, not exact pressure-temperature boundaries.

Facies depend on pressure as well as temperature. Blueschist is characteristically high-pressure/low-temperature, while hornfels is associated with low-pressure contact metamorphism. Vibration of the basilar membrane causes hair bundles at apex of hair cell to 
bend back and forth against one another. As the stereocilia bend, the transduction 
channels are opened, allowing K+ from the endolymph to enter the hair cell 
cytosol. This produces a depolarizing receptor potential, which causes voltage 
gated Ca2+ channels to open. Inflow of Ca2+ triggers exocytosis of synaptic 
vesicles containing neurotransmitters.

criteria.answer: No; the edible taproot does not regrow once removed.
The carrot top may grow greens, but that does not regenerate the harvested taproot.
No, not from the fruit scrap.
Cavendish bananas are propagated by pups or suckers from the rhizome, which can be separated from the parent.
The intact root/basal structures regrow leaves, including in water.
The crown / top leaves can root and develop into a new plant.
Retained basal tissue can produce new leaves.
It is potentially poisonous; the key says not to eat it.
Sprouting/greening can accompany elevated toxic glycoalkaloids such as solanine. Chlorophyll gives green color but is not itself the toxin.
Osmosis replenishes cell water and turgor pressure, restoring rigidity.
Genetic diversity reduces the chance that one pathogen wipes out the entire crop.
Different susceptibility/resistance among plants means some can survive. The source’s claim that Gros Michel is extinct is not required for credit.
Trade/colonization spread potatoes from South America, and farmers selected less-bitter, lower-glycoalkaloid tubers.
A relevant further explanation, such as abundant yields encouraging cultivation and adoption.
Different crops use/replenish nutrients differently, helping maintain soil fertility and yield.
Explain a relevant benefit such as reduced erosion, alternating deep/shallow roots, or avoiding repeated depletion of the same nutrients.

A valid example on each side: improved nutrition such as provitamin-A Golden Rice, and economic concerns such as seed licensing costs or dependence on suppliers. Do not require unsupported claims that every GMO seed is sterile.
Explain how the examples affect people or agricultural production; accept other scientifically valid examples.
Pioneer organisms / lichens where rock is exposed, and annuals, grasses and later perennial plants as suitable.
Explain how conditions and soil availability influence recovery; secondary succession on remaining soil need not begin with lichens.
Root support can come from other substrates and essential mineral nutrients can be supplied in water.
Explain how nutrient solution and suitable root conditions fulfill functions normally provided by soil.
A suitable nutrient mixture providing nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients.
Explain supplying the nutrients in solution / liquid fertilizer; accept biologically appropriate nitrogen forms and additional essential minerals.
Rice paddies or cranberry bogs, or another valid example.
Explain how the crop is cultivated with partial/substantial water exposure; avoid implying that cranberry vines are permanently submerged.
Yes: their waste supplies nitrogen compounds that can support plant growth.

Fish still need an external food supply; suitable microbial processing and management are needed. Accept a correctly explained aquaponic mutual benefit; the source’s categorical denial of symbiosis is not required.
Hydroponics is a plant cultivation method using nutrient solution; aquaculture cultivates aquatic organisms and can include different systems.

criteria.answer:
Lane 2 may have supercoiled DNA (1). Supercoiled DNA occurs when the DNA helix twists
 on itself (1). This creates DNA molecules which are smaller than other arrangements of DNA
 (1); since these fragments are smaller, they are able to travel further through the agarose gel
 (1).

Dosage compensation (1) is the process by which 1 X chromosome becomes inactivated
 (lyonization) (1), preventing excessive amounts of X gene products from being produced (1).

No, these findings should not surprise them (1) because X inactivation is random (1),
 meaning the unhealthy X chromosome could be permanently silenced (1), resulting in no
 disease being present in some of the cells (1).
 a) Any mention (with an explanation) of mosaicism can earn the 3rd and 4th point.

 OR

 Yes, these findings should surprise them (1) X inactivation would not matter if the woman is
 carrying 2 unhealthy X chromosomes (1). X inactivation only silences 1 out of 2 X
 chromosomes (1) so at least 1 unhealthy X chromosome is being used to code for products
 (1).

Response must mention or indicate that since the frequency of alleles does not change, the
 population can be assumed to be under H.W. equilibrium. (1)
 a) Writing both H.W. formulas in the response earns this point

 q=3/80=0.0375 (1)
 p+q=1 → p=0.9625 (1)
 p2+2pq+q2=1
 (0.9625)2+2(0.0375)(0.9625)+(0.0375)2=1
 Incidence of cystic fibrosis = 0.03752=0.00140625 or roughly 0.0014 (1)

Acetylation increases gene expression (1). DNA is wrapped around positively charged
 histones. Acetylation neutralizes the positive charge (1) by adding an acetyl group to lysine
 residue on the histones (1). This allows for DNA to have a more relaxed chromatin structure
 (euchromatin) (1), making the DNA more accessible to relevant enzymes/proteins (1).

AB, aB, Ab, and ab are the possible genotypes of the gamete (1). There are multiple
 possibilities because homologous chromosomes are independently assorted during metaphase
 I (1). Gametes have fewer alleles than their parents because in anaphase I, homologous
 chromosomes are separated and in anaphase II, sister chromatids are separated (2; 1 point for
 each separation mentioned).
Polyadenylation, addition of a 5′ GTP cap, and mRNA splicing

a) All-or-nothing grading; if the error is that they write the specific genes for the lac
 operon instead of structural gene, then deduct 1 point only. 5 points total. Diagram order left to right: Promoter, Regulatory Gene, Promoter, Operator, Structural Gene.

5’ A U G C G G C A U A A G 3’ → (1) for a correct mRNA sequence
 a) Indication of top strand being used for transcription (1) along with correct primes (1)
 (N terminus) Formyl-methionine–arginine–histidine–lysine (C terminus)
 b) 6 total points; 1 per amino acid; 1 additional point for having the entire strand correct;
 1 point for including N and C terminus in the correct places
 c) Just methionine for the first amino acid is not considered correct

The fluorescent gene allows us to monitor whether or not the gene is being transcribed (1)
 since the green promoter is only active when the operon before it is active (1). If the
 fluorescent protein is present, we know that the gene has been transcribed (1).

Standard PCR (1)
 Step 1: Denaturing involves using high temperatures to cause DNA to break into single
 strands (95 deg C) (1)
 Step 2: Annealing allows for primers to anneal to ssDNA at lower temperatures (55 deg C)
 (1)
 Step 3: Elongation involves synthesis of new strands by Taq polymerase (72 deg C) (1)
 a) Error of margin for temperatures is +/- 5 deg C
 b) Accept other PCR methods which are used for amplification of DNA (use the internet
 to verify temperatures with the same error margin with the same scoring rubric of 1
 point per step)

Taq polymerase (1) is useful because it does not denature at higher temperatures than human
 polymerase(1), allowing for elongation to occur and creating identical copies of the DNA.
 a) If the answer to #5 is a PCR method which does not use taq polymerase specifically
 (e.g. pfu PCR), grade the answer as:
 i) Name of the enzyme (1)
 ii) Similar/same reasoning as the rubric (1) OR specifying an advantage of the
 PCR method (e.g. pfu PCR has a higher accuracy due to proofreading
 functions) (1)

Bacteria replicate faster than eukaryotic cells which allows the plasmid to be cloned many
 times rapidly (1). The origin of replication (ori) of plasmids are not compatible with
 eukaryotic cells (1).
 a) Answers must say bacterial cells to be eligible for credit.

questions.prompt:
At Palo Alto High school, there is a major seagull population. Biology students at PALY discovered 
 an allele that alters the bird’s taste preferences called s . Seagulls with homozygous dominant 
 alleles crave savory school lunches while seagulls with homozygous recessive genotypes attack 
 students for sweets. If the seagull is heterozygous for the allele, they enjoy BOTH sweet and 
 savory school lunches, no students are safe. 
 a. If 49% of the bird population enjoyed only sweet foods, and assuming the 
 population is in Hardy Weinberg equilibrium, what percentage of the 
 population enjoys ONLY SAVORY FOOD?(Show your work, 3pts) 
 b. What percentage of the seagull population enjoys stealing both savory and sweet 
 food?(Show your work, 2pts) Describe any required drawing in labeled text.

criteria.answer:
Morbidity refers to the prevalence or incidence of a disease, while mortality refers to the
 rate of death attributed to a certain condition or population.

Poor sewage systems, failure to sanitize surfaces, not washing hands, undercooking food,
 improper food storage

Patients are assembled on the basis of some common experience and are then monitored
 for a specified amount of time at regular intervals until they develop the outcome of
 interest or the follow-up period ends

Relative risk is the association between the exposure and outcome, attributable risk
 estimates how many observed cases can be linked to the exposure.

[3 pts]
 Pregnant women/newborns, elderly populations, immunodeficient adults [1 pt each]

[3 pts]
 Unpasteurized dairy products, ready-to-eat deli meats, raw fruits and vegetables [1 pt
 each]

[3 pts]
 Nausea, diarrhea, fever, muscle aches, flu-like symptoms [grader’s discretion]

[8 pts]
 Cases Controls
 Ate at Yorkside 15 20
 Did not eat at Yorkside 10 20
 25 40

 Cases Controls

 Did not eat at Salsa Fresca 20 28
 25 40

 Yorkside: !"∗$% = 1.5
 $%∗!%

 !$∗$% !$
 Yorkside has a higher odds ratio, so it is more likely. [1 pt for each statement]

[2 pts]
 Not all infected patients may have reported, other sources of infection may have been
 unaccounted for, etc [grader’s discretion]

[5 pts]
 • Identify food items served during the implicated time period.
 • Determine whether any kitchen staff or their family members were ill at the time
 of the outbreak
 • Describe handwashing facilities at the cafeteria and routine hygienic practices of
 foodhandlers
 • Collect stool specimens from all foodhandlers
 • Watch or reconstruct kitchen procedures in days leading up to the implicated time
 period, in order to identify any unusual occurences or departures from routine
 during the outbreak
 • Outline work schedules for foodhandlers during the implicated period and
 identify who was responsible for what on which days
 • Get recipes for food items served during the implicated time period and identify
 the ingredients and their sources
 [1 pt each, up to 5]

[2 pts]
 Primary case patient: patient zero, direct exposure to contaminated food or surfaces
 Secondary case patient: infected by spread from already affected patients via droplets or
 contact [1 pt each]
Listeria monocytogenes (2 tie points only if the entire name is correct). L. ivanovii or L. grayi earns one tie point.

One process described in detail. RT-PCR first reverse-transcribes viral RNA to cDNA, then amplifies a specific sequence using primers, nucleotides and polymerase through thermal cycles. The source also accepts a detailed antibody test or culture description; retain instructor discretion for alternatives.

An onset curve has three bins with counts 6, 8, and 2.
A report-date curve would incorrectly look like 16 simultaneous reports if interpreted as onset.
Use onset timing to generate source hypotheses and assess completeness before claiming the source.
The time variable changes the meaning of the curve.

public health recommendations that rely on the evidence.

case within the outbreak that researchers discovered, Bob is the _____________ of the outbreak.

questions.prompt: Authored written substitute for unavailable source material: Why not compute risk from an ordinary case-control sample fraction?
questions.context:
Unit: Identifying study designs.
Worked-case data: Investigators interview every attendee on a banquet roster after an outbreak and compare illness by food consumed. Identify the design.

criteria.answer: Accept 6–15 hours for diarrheal Bacillus cereus, as keyed; also accept the shorter roughly 0.5–6-hour emetic incubation when distinguished. Two points for a valid form/range.
Contact, vehicle and vector transmission. Accept equivalent recognized transmission modes.
a Age 80 or older; b All ages; c approximately 47–53%. One point each; use the supplied hospitalization graphs.

Selection is based on banquet attendance, not illness status.
Exposure and outcome are reconstructed for the full defined cohort.
Food-specific risks and RR can be estimated if ascertainment and denominators are adequate.
This is a retrospective cohort, despite collecting the information after the event.

a 48/60=.80 (2); b 18/40=.45 (2); c .80/.45=1.78 (2); d exposed cohort has about 1.78 times the risk, without proving causation (2); e cohort (1); f three valid symptoms such as diarrhea, cramps, nausea, fever or vomiting (2).

a OR=(25*63)/(32*14)=3.52 (2); b cases have about 3.52 times the odds of exposure compared with controls, equivalently an exposure–disease odds association, not directly 3.52 times the risk (2); c case-control (1); d retrospective (1); e Mantel–Haenszel stratified/adjusted odds ratio (1).

An onset curve has three bins with counts 6, 8, and 2.
A report-date curve would incorrectly look like 16 simultaneous reports if interpreted as onset.
Use onset timing to generate source hypotheses and assess completeness before claiming the source.
The time variable changes the meaning of the curve.

Create a clear, operational revised definition using the listed clinical findings and IgM anti-HAV evidence. A defensible definition can require acute onset plus compatible symptoms and positive IgM anti-HAV. Do not force an internally contradictory definition.

Count consistently with the definition proposed in Q9 and the supplied table. All six are IgM-HAV-positive; only four have jaundice. A definition requiring jaundice therefore cannot yield six. Award the point for a correct count under the student’s explicit criteria.
IgM antibody to hepatitis A virus; a marker used in assessing recent/acute HAV infection in the appropriate clinical context.

a Determine whether food refrigeration was adequately cold to limit bacterial growth (2); b determine whether cooking temperatures could kill vegetative bacteria (2). Fat temperature alone does not guarantee food-center temperature or destruction of preformed toxins.

Name a distinct risk factor and mechanism: e.g. cracked surface harbors microbes, putrefied meat contaminates grinder, missing handwashing promotes transfer, or 68 F refrigerator permits growth. One point identification, one explanation.
Name a second distinct risk factor and explain its mechanism, as in Q14. Do not duplicate the same factor for additional credit.
Name a third distinct risk factor and explain its mechanism, as in Q14. Do not duplicate earlier factors.

Coliform testing detects/counts indicator bacteria and helps assess water sanitation or contamination. Total coliform presence is not direct proof of a specific pathogen; fecal indicators are more specific to fecal contamination.

Random error is chance variation; confounding is distortion by a third factor related to exposure and outcome. Accept systematic versus random error if explained, since confounding is a bias rather than a non-bias error.
Selection bias arises from differential inclusion; information bias from systematic measurement/classification errors. Give an example of each.
Clostridium perfringens bacterial; Mucor circinelloides fungal; shigellosis bacterial; listeriosis bacterial; aspergillosis fungal; candidiasis fungal.
Investigators choose case/control numbers; those fractions do not represent source-population disease occurrence.

questions.prompt: Which of the five statements demonstrates active immunity? Explain the yes/no choices.
questions.context:

 DO NOT WRITE BELOW THIS LINE Final Score: _________/48 Rank Number: Tiebreaker Score: _________/16 

Test begins on this page. 1. For the following statements, determine whether each one correctly demonstrates ACTIVE immunity (a simple yes/no will suffice): (3 points total) a. A tribal population avoids consumption of a known poisonous mushroom and thus never experiences the effects caused by eating it. b. Individuals inflicted with sickle-cell disease have natural immunity to the human immunodeficiency virus due to the inability of the virus to reproduce on the afflicted blood cells. c. Children living in the United States rarely develop meningococcal disease due to vaccines given at a young age. d. A man regularly eats a healthy diet and exercise and thus is at reduced risk for heart disease. e. A tribe in one location is never subjected to diseases of another location and thus never experiences the effects of that disease. 2. Briefly describe the chain of infection epidemiological triad (5 points): 3. Many individuals in a nation reported symptoms of the (fictional) disease Heloniogitis, a larger number than occurred in the past five years. A study was conducted in the area and found that there was not a statistically significant difference between the number of afflicted individuals and the expected number of afflictions in the area. a. Is this an outbreak? (yes or no only) (2 points) 
4. In a separate case, there was a confirmed salmonella outbreak in an elementary school. A study was performed and found that 17 out of the 20 of the afflicted students had eaten the tomato salad served by the school cafeteria. In the study, an odds ratio of 1.01 was found using a confidence interval of 95%. No other common risk factors were able to be identified. a. With the information provided by the study, can the school’s tomato salad be pinpointed as the source of the outbreak? Why or why not? (3 points) b. What does the odds ratio tell us about a possible connection between the tomato salad and the salmonella outbreak? (4 points) 5. Name 3 possible ways a pathogen may enter the human body (5 points). 6. Give TWO examples of each of the following: a. Biological cause for disease (2 points) b. Chemical cause for disease (2 points) c. Physical cause for disease (2 points)

Collect two samples without bubbles; perform and record the first dissolved oxygen test; store the other sample in darkness for five days; test its DO and record; subtract day-five DO from day-one DO.

All species except mosquito larvae cannot survive.
A general overall health assessment: quick, easy and cheap.
Water is too cloudy for photosynthetic organisms to function, so the food web can collapse.
Reduce nutrient application losses or improve wastewater nutrient removal, with local validation.

questions.label: repair-case
questions.prompt: Authored written substitute for unavailable source material: Define “Point source” in the context of Water Quality.

criteria.answer: Any two distinct factors, one point each: water temperature, salinity, atmospheric pressure, biological photosynthesis/respiration/decomposition, or mixing/aeration. Explain direction if discussed; cooler water and lower salinity generally allow more dissolved oxygen.

A human source of suspended material that increases turbidity, such as construction/erosion runoff, urban stormwater, industrial discharge or disturbed sediment. The source also lists oil and wastes; accept these when the response explains their effect on clarity.

A disease associated with fecally contaminated drinking water, for example dysentery, typhoid fever, gastroenteritis, hepatitis A, cholera or giardiasis. Fecal coliforms are indicators; they do not necessarily cause each named disease.

Biochemical (or biological) oxygen demand: dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing organic matter over the specified incubation period. Both the expansion and meaning are required within one point.

Any three distinct effects, one point each: reduced light/photosynthesis, impaired plant growth, increased water heating, gill interference, reduced visual feeding, aesthetic impairment, or protection/transport of microbes or pollutants. Avoid duplicate descriptions of the same effect.
Females release eggs over water or attach egg masses to rocks/vegetation by water; accept a biologically valid stonefly oviposition method.
Diapause, delayed development or hatching until suitable conditions.

Moist or wet habitats, including stream margins, wetlands or damp soil/vegetation; many occur in humid or high-elevation/northern settings. Do not require all habitats listed in the key for every species.
The key describes moderately clean water. Crane-fly tolerance varies by species; accept a qualified intermediate-tolerance indicator interpretation rather than a universal claim of pristine water.
Adult life is typically a few days to roughly two weeks; the aquatic/soil larval stage is longer.

Many water boatmen graze algae/plant material and detritus; some also consume small invertebrates, so herbivory, detritivory or omnivory is acceptable. The source’s zoophagy-only answer is too restrictive; accept a correct explanation of species-dependent animal feeding.
They carry a trapped air supply under the wings/around the body and obtain oxygen from it while submerged, replenishing at the surface.

Males attract mates with sound/stridulation, produced by rubbing specialized body structures. The key describes forelegs against the head; accept other correctly explained species-specific stridulatory structures.
Vegetative reproduction by runners/stolons producing daughter plants; accept equivalent clonal offshoot description.
Dense invasive mats shade submerged plants, restrict flow, outcompete native species and may lower oxygen during respiration/decomposition. Any valid harmful water-quality effect earns the point.

Warming can initially increase growth of tolerant plants/algae, but excessive heat can stress or kill sensitive plants, reduce oxygen availability and alter community composition. Accept a scientifically sound effect with appropriate qualification.

An appropriate example is a manatee using warm-water refuges during cold weather, or a warm-tolerant aquatic plant such as Egeria densa or parrot’s feather where local conditions favor it. Do not treat thermal pollution as universally beneficial. Brook trout are cold-water fish and do not automatically benefit from warming.

pH=-log10(10^-5.8)=5.8 (1 point). This is acidic and may harm sensitive species, but can support acid-tolerant organisms; pH alone does not establish that no life can survive (1 point). The key’s blanket no-life claim is corrected.

alignment: The source freshwater rotation differs from the 2027 marine/estuary and coral-reef organism focus. Monitoring and treatment concepts overlap.

Original tiebreakers and intentionally excluded duplicate items retain their original treatment. Read the complete original paper, including diagrams and tables. Answer every labeled part. Use the appended repair pages for those items; the original archived pages are preserved. Replacement weights are practice weights; this total is not the historical tournament score. All three sections are converted: eight ecology questions, eight organism IDs plus their eight historical tolerance classes, and 15 analysis questions (39 fields). Published weights total 51. Analysis 9 is unscored because TDS is confused with suspended material/turbidity; Analysis 12 is unscored because the wording confuses alkalinity with pH-dependent ammonia toxicity. Available score is 49. The energy-pyramid answer is corrected to 124.2 J as requested to the nearest tenth, rather than the rounded 124 J in the key. The 1–5 organism classes are the paper’s historical water-quality tolerance groups, not taxonomic classes or the current rules roster. No named competition or tier is inferred.

criteria.answer: Biomagnification: an increase in persistent pollutant concentration at successive trophic levels.
Assuming the standard 10% energy-transfer model shown in the pyramid: 12420×0.1²=124.2 J in predators. The key rounds this to 124 J, but the prompt asks to the nearest tenth.
Plants decrease: removing predators allows herbivores to increase and consume more plants.
Top predators: tertiary consumers (fourth trophic level); predators: secondary consumers (third); herbivores: primary consumers (second); plants: primary producers (first).

The source key expects about 110% oxygen saturation. This is a historical screening threshold; supersaturation risk depends on species, exposure and total dissolved-gas conditions rather than a universal exact oxygen threshold.
Methemoglobinemia, commonly called blue baby syndrome.
Fecal contamination and possible associated pathogens; fecal coliforms are indicators rather than proof of a specific pathogen.
Secondary treatment, including biological sludge processing; anaerobic digestion stabilizes sludge and may occur as a separate sludge-treatment stage.
pH is -log10 of hydrogen-ion activity (approximately concentration in dilute solution), measuring acidity/basicity. Do not define it merely as all dissolved ions.
6 degrees Celsius: colder water generally holds more dissolved oxygen at equal salinity/pressure.
About 4 degrees Celsius (approximately 3.98°C for pure freshwater at atmospheric pressure).
Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), following the key’s intended turbidity answer to question 9.
0.17, the dissolved-oxygen weighting factor used in the source’s NSF-style water-quality index.
Flow and a defined time interval.
Parts per thousand (ppt), the source’s salinity unit.
States set applicable water-quality standards subject to federal Clean Water Act requirements and EPA oversight; do not interpret this as excluding tribal or federal roles.

criteria.answer: kappa-mechanism: Explain that "kappa" refers to opacity. In the pulsation zone, Helium (He^+) is ionized to He^++ as the star contracts. Energy Trap: Ionized Helium is more opaque, trapping radiation and increasing internal pressure, which pushes the outer layers outward.Expansion & Cooling: As the star expands, it cools, and the Helium recombines (He^++ back to He^+), becoming transparent and allowing radiation to escape. Narrow Range: This only works in a speciﬁc temperature range where the Helium ionization zone is at the correct depth to drive the entire atmosphere.

O-type Stars: High surface temperatures (>30,000 K) cause atoms to be highly ionized. Features include He II (ionized helium) lines. M-type Stars: Cooler temperatures (<3,700 K) allow molecules to remain intact. Features include prominent Titanium Oxide (TiO) absorption bands. Molecular Dissociation: Explain that O-type stars have the same elements, but the intense heat provides enough energy to break molecular bonds (dissociation), meaning molecules like TiO cannot exist.

Core State: Core Hydrogen is exhausted, leaving an inert Helium core that begins to contract under gravity. Shell Burning: Hydrogen fusion moves to a shell surrounding the core, which provides the high luminosity and pressure that expands the envelope. Red Giant Growth: The envelope expands and cools (moving the star to the right), while the core becomes "electron degenerate." Degeneracy: In the core, electrons are packed so tightly that the Pauli Exclusion Principle provides pressure independent of temperature, preventing further collapse until the Helium Flash.

X-Ray (High Energy): Shows the "inner" nebula and the torus/jets. This emission is from the most energetic electrons recently accelerated by the pulsar. Radio (Low Energy): Shows the "outer" and more diffuse nebula. These are older electrons that have migrated further away and lost energy over time. Synchrotron Radiation: Both wavelengths are produced by electrons spiraling in magnetic ﬁelds; the difference in appearance is due to the electron's energy decay (synchrotron cooling).

Mie Scattering/Extinction: Dust grains are roughly the size of blue light wavelengths, so they scatter/absorb blue light more effectively than red (reddening). Optical Void: In the visible spectrum, the density of the dust is high enough to create inﬁnite optical depth (total obscuration). Infrared Advantage: IR wavelengths are much longer than the dust grain size, allowing them to pass through the cloud without being scattered. Protostar Identiﬁcation: IR allows us to see the thermal heat signature of the collapsing core (protostar) which is otherwise hidden.

Type II (Hydrogen Lines): Progenitor is a massive star (>8 M.) that retained its Hydrogen envelope before core collapse. Type Ia (Silicon, No Hydrogen): Progenitor is a White Dwarf in a binary system that reached the Chandrasekhar limit. It has no Hydrogen because White Dwarfs are the exposed cores of former stars. Evolutionary Path: Type II involves iron core collapse; Type Ia involves a thermonuclear runaway of Carbon/Oxygen.

Physical Structure: The "infrared excess" is caused by a circumstellar/protoplanetary disk of gas and dust that absorbs starlight and re-emits it as heat (IR). Evolutionary Stage: Unlike a protostar, a T Tauri star is visible in the optical, has cleared much of its "envelope," but is still contracting toward the Main Sequence. Hydrostatic Equilibrium: T Tauri stars have achieved a degree of hydrostatic balance but are powered by gravitational contraction rather than Hydrogen fusion.

Gravitational Settling: Because gravity is so intense, heavy elements (metals) sink to the center, leaving the lightest elements (H or He) at the surface. Spectral Types: DA white dwarfs have Hydrogen-rich atmospheres; DB have Helium-rich atmospheres. Janus Transition: Janus challenges this by showing "patches" or transitions, suggesting that as a star cools, convective zones can reach deep enough to "dredge up" buried Helium and mix the atmosphere.

Interacting Winds: A fast, thin wind from the hot white dwarf core catches up to the slow, dense wind ejected earlier during the AGB phase (the "snowplow" effect). Cometary Knots: These are dense clumps of molecular gas protected from the central star’s ionizing radiation by their own shadows, creating "tails" pointing away from the star. Ionization Fronts: The distinct "ring" shape is often an illusion of a 3D shell where the edges appear thicker from our line of sight.

Potential Energy Conversion: As matter falls from the donor star toward the compact object, it loses gravitational potential energy, which is converted into heat (kinetic energy). Accretion Disk Friction: Friction between different layers of the disk (differential rotation) generates temperatures in the millions of Kelvin. Wien’s Law: Because the temperature is so high (10^6 - 10^7 K), the peak wavelength of emission shifts into the X-ray part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

criteria.answer: Phosphorus and nitrogen, as it comes from agricultural fertilizers and residential runoff. The nitrogen and phosphorus (especially) can lead to watershed eutrophication, eventually leading to “dead zones”.
Dendritic drainage patterns are the most common drainage pattern.
Anastomose channels are basically braided stream channels, but they don’t divide or reconnect as easily as braided stream channels.
Waterfalls are usually formed when water flowing above harder rock erodes away at softer rock, downcutting it.

Lake Tanganyika was formed as a part of the western branch of the East African Rift, thus making it a rift lake. As how other rift lakes are formed, Lake Tanganyika was most likely formed from the rifting and subsidence of parts of the African plate ~9-12 million years ago.

sediment budget is difficult to calculate because it is difficult to calculate the exact amount of sediment added or subtracted from a certain area and all the sources and sinks of sediment must be taken into account.

The rapidly growing population needed a dam to provide enough water. The construction of a high dam at Aswan tampered with the river’s delicate flow patterns, thus diminishing the seasonal flooding at the bank. The controlled outflow of water from the dam into Lake Nasser meant that it accumulated ~98% of the suspended sediment usually carried downstream. This is not good as agriculture required the rich sediment deposited when the river used to seasonally flood, leading to increased fertilizer use which leads to higher water pollution.
gravel, sand, silt, clay, and salts
Darcy’s law states that the negative of permeability/dynamic viscosity of the fluid multiplied by the pressure drop is equal to the instantaneous flow rate of a fluid.
The “fried egg” formation was formed when workers accidentally snapped off two stalagmites, and tourists at Luray Caverns have eroded the stalagmites into the “fried egg” shape.

Both stalagmites & stalactites are formed when calcite salts precipitates from groundwater on cave walls; stalagmites precipitate from the floor up, while stalactites precipitate from the roof of the cave and up, almost like icicles.
Yes, as after the volcano erupts and the depression is formed, the lake forms and clay called hectorite can accumulate.
The water flows back into watersheds, is absorbed into the ground as groundwater, and erodes Earth’s surfaces as it flows back into watersheds.

Karst formations are formed when soft, water-soluble bedrock such as limestone, dolomite, gypsum, & marble gets dissolved by running water, forming distinct features such as sinkholes, springs, and streams.
Sinkholes can be from either the erosion or removal of soluble bedrock (i.e. limestone) from running water, collapse of a cave roof, lowering of a water table, or overwithdrawal of groundwater.

The photo shows a tidal marsh. Tidal marshes form in areas that are sheltered from waves, and they drain and flood based off the tidal pattern of the adjacent watershed (i.e. rivers, estuaries, oceans). They are found along rivers, coasts, or seas, and can be freshwater or saline.

Groundwater is naturally filtered as it passes through layers of material and porous soil--groundwater is generally cleaner than surface water since surface water has chemicals, pollutants, organisms, and other materials that aren’t filtered out like groundwater. Groundwater is usually safe to drink unlike surface water.
No (generally), as the particles of silt are larger than clay, thus meaning silt has more pore space than clay, on average.

The salt levels in seawater is way too high for the human body as human kidneys cannot get rid of the excess salt, plus seawater is dehydrating; there is no overarching issued “safe” level of dissolved salt in drinking water, USGS says to not exceed levels above 500 mg/L to avoid the salty taste.
Seasonal lakes are named ephemeral lakes since “ephemeral” means “lasting temporarily”, and seasonal lakes only hold water for short periods, thus ephemeral describes seasonal lakes well.
A black-and-white Secchi disk is generally used to measure freshwater turbidity.
Xeriscaping, especially with native plants, reduces the amount of fertilizers and pesticides that get washed up into local watersheds, and, most importantly, conserves water.

Asian Carp outcompetes native animals, disrupting the ecosystem. Plus, they can survive in lower quality water, killing off sensitive indicator organisms. Asian Carp also jump out of water to evade threats, which can injure people paddling in the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Lastly, they cost the Mississippi River area’s fishing industry $7 billion annually by outcompeting native fish (those that are usually caught and sold).

The Chesapeake Bay supplies a lot of seafood and recreational spots that many states rely on for economy, and the wetlands and watersheds shelter diverse communities of life and soften coastal storms.

The likelihood of droughts occurring are predicted by monitoring rainfall, river flow, and soil moisture. The water table changes, as the water table and aquifers rely on rainfall to replenish the levels of the water. The height of the water table drops as the rate water is pumped from the ground exceeds the rate the water can be replenished, thus the ground subsides and sinks.
An aquifer is a layer of underground permeable rock that holds groundwater.

Groundwater drilling, or groundwater extraction causes land subsidence, lack of surface water, and lowered water quality in aquifers. If there is too much extraction of groundwater, the water table lowers thus leading to wells not being able to reach groundwater; watersheds like rivers that connect to groundwater will also have the water supply diminished. Thus, no, groundwater extraction is not ethical for the environment.

Land subsidence is sometimes due to the lowering of the water table or excess pumping of groundwater; the sediments that hold up the land with water now partially lowers due to the loss of groundwater, causing land to drop and changing the topographic gradient. Land subsidence also reduces aquifers’ abilities to store water, most likely changing the water quality and altering underground sediments.

Arsenic gets into drinking water sources either naturally or artificially from industrial waste and agricultural pollution (certain fertilizers contain arsenic). Antimony gets into drinking water often from being dissolved in metal plumbing/fittings.
the unsaturated zone is usually 0-100+ m underground, depending on climate and land type.
The water balance equation is an important part of hydrology as it displays the system of hydrology as a whole using the conservation of mass.
Labels: River, Perched water table, Unsaturated zone, Water table, Aquifer (labeled diagram in the published key; any order accepted).

Deforestation, poorly managed construction sites, winter road sanding, erosion/exposed soil, overgrazing/bad agricultural practice all lead up to excess weathering/erosion of surface sediments. The sediment eventually washes up into rivers and other watersheds, leading to excess sediments in watersheds. Dams also alter the patterns of sediment transport, adding on to the problem.

Excess sediment leads to altered water depth and altered water flow, thus making watersheds more difficult to navigate. Water quality also goes down, such as increased turbidity, TDS (total dissolved solids), and TSS (total suspended solids). The extra sediment also disrupts the balance of watershed ecosystems, harming delicate indicator species and others alike.

Firstly, flow patterns are disrupted, thus affecting habitats as sediment transport patterns change. Adding on, water quality factors such as dissolved oxygen levels and temperature are changed. Cold, oxygen-deprived water is released from the reservoir bottom, affecting water quality. Sediments, logs, gravel, etc. can be trapped in dams, creating pools downstream and burying the riverbeds where fish spawn.

Disrupted flow patterns affect migrating fish and disrupt the fragile ecosystem balance. Dissolved oxygen levels and temperatures are especially affected: surface water annual temperature variation increases while deep water annual temperature variation does the opposite; this is not good for sensitive species. Temperature also affects dissolved oxygen levels, thus leading to algal blooms and lower dissolved oxygen levels. Dams block rivers from migrating fish, disrupting the surrounding ecosystem once again.

1) Excess nutrients (ammonia/ammonium, nitrates, phosphates) and sediments are introduced to a watershed (mainly lakes), whether through human activity (i.e. an overabundance of fertilizer washing into a local lake) or naturally. 2) The introduction of abnormal levels of nutrients lead to algae rapidly blooming. This algal bloom; the water appears murky, covered in “scum” (the algae), and overall disgusting. Often, sediment washes in too, thus continuing the negative feedback loop of more algae growing.
3) Algae blocks sunlight from reaching the bottom of the affected area & uses up a lot of oxygen. 4) Eventually, the water becomes so depleted of oxygen organisms it becomes a “dead zone”.

It is usually part of the water table as the part where water table that naturally meets the surface is considered still a water table but it could be a watershed such as a stream, river, or lake. If we look at it a different way, it is not considered part of a water table as a watershed is a drainage basin where all precipitation drains to an endorheic basin, while a water table is the horizontal depth of the top of the aquifer. Thus, no and yes.
Meanders are formed when water erodes sediment in the outer bank of a stream.
They are mildly common especially in the middle & lower course of a bridge.
Each natural lake is formed when a depression called a lake basin gets filled in with water, or from an existing body of water. The way the lake basin forms varies.

Cirque/tarn lakes, Glacial lakes, Rock hollow lakes, Volcanic lakes, Meteorite lakes, Solution lakes, Fluvial lakes, Oxbow lakes, Landslide lakes, Tectonic lakes, Aeolian lakes, Freshwater lakes, Organic/animal-made lakes, Saline lakes, Barrier lakes, Rift valley lakes, Karst lakes, Wind deflation lakes, Human-made/artificial lakes, permanent lakes, temporary lakes (and their respective formation mechanisms as detailed in the key).

Groundwater pumping for oil & gas extraction, groundwater extraction, contamination that seeps into the ground such as dumping toxic waste or landfill/waste disposal or agricultural contaminants, urban & industrial discharges all human activities that affects groundwater

Groundwater pumping contaminates groundwater and alters how water moves between a watershed, aquifer, and groundwater by intercepting groundwater flow that discharges into the surface-water body, or increasing the rate of water movement from the surface-watershed into an aquifer, leading to an aquifer holding too much water that discharges to surface watersheds that exacerbates erosion, altering aquatic life. Groundwater extraction leads to land subsidence and changes in topography; contaminants from things such as landfill waste can seep into the groundwater, again discharging to surrounding soil and watersheds, being toxic to life, decreasing ground- and surface- water quality; urban and industrial discharge might have similar effects to landfill waste.

criteria.answer: A pycnocline is a rapid density-gradient layer; a thermocline is a rapid temperature-gradient layer. The source incorrectly substituted pressure for density.

Natural disasters
 a. El Niño happens when there are sea surface anomalies greater than 0.5 deg. C across the
 central tropical Pacific ocean.
 b. El Niño Conditions are temporary signs that the tropical Pacific Ocean is starting to warm
 abnormally in a period of less than five months. An El Niño episode is a fully developed
 and sustained climate pattern characterized by significant and widespread warming of sea
 surface temperatures (SSTs) in the tropical Pacific which lasts for 5 months or longer.
 c. Warm tropical water replaces the cold water used to support populations of fish.
 d. El niño occurs when there is an abnormal amount of warm water, whereas la niña occurs
 when there is an abnormal amount of cold water.
 e. Upwelling is when cold, nutrient-rich water rises up to the surface to support marine
 ecosystems. El Niño weakens upwelling along eastern boundaries, while La Niña
 strengthens upwelling. El Niño causes phytoplankton decline and impacts zooplankton,
 fish, seabirds, and marine mammals, while La Niña increases plankton populations and
 increases the populations of these animal populations.

Boundary types
 a. Plates move away from each other. rift zones, mid-ocean ridges, and expanding ocean
 basins
 b. Pressure is reduced on the mantle below and magma flows out.
 c. Many answers apply. The most common answer should be mid-atlantic ridge.
 d. Rift-structure
 e. Ocean-water flows in and can cause rivers to form or affect bodies of water.

Waves
 a. Wave crest
 b. Wave trough
 c. One half the distance between the crest and the trough.
 d. Very small waves with very small wavelengths.
 e. Wind pressures on the water.
 f. Waves that move back and forth (oscillate) vertically. The wave appears like it’s moving
 forwards when it’s not.

Ocean sediments
 a. Lithogenous/terrigenous sediment
 b. Near continental margins
 c. Biogenous sediment
 d. Calcareous deposits from shells of marine organisms. Answers vary, though.
 e. Precipitating from the ocean water.
 f. Lithogenous and biogenous
 g. Cosmogenous sediment.

Surface currents
 a. Deflected to the left in the southern hemisphere or counter-clockwise direction
 b. Eastern boundary currents
 

 c. Western boundary currents are faster, narrower, warmer and deeper than Eastern currents.
 Eastern boundary currents are relatively slower, broader, colder, and shallower than
 Western currents.
 d. The Gulf Stream is the Western boundary current that flows north along the eastern coast
 of the US.
 e. A gyre is classified as a big system of rotating ocean currents formed through the coriolis
 force, landmasses, and global wind circulation.
 f. Surface currents help regulate marine ecosystems through nutrient cycling and weather
 patterns such as precipitation.

Geostrophic and ekman balances
 a. Differences in the water’s height and therefore pressure across a horizontal region.
 Factors like variations in water density (due to temperature and salinity differences)
 create these pressure differences. This is because a higher density would result in a
 greater pressure gradient, whereas a smaller density results in a smaller pressure gradient.
 These pressure gradients determine the strength of a current.
 b. The pressure gradient always acts perpendicular to the isobars and from areas of high
 pressure to low pressure.
 c. The wind stress and coriolis effect produce the forty five degree angle in the ekman layer.
 d. The ekman balance is comprised of wind stress frictional forces and the coriolis force
 while the geostrophic balance is comprised of the pressure gradient force and the coriolis
 force.the ekman balance describes a smaller scale of water flow while geostrophic
 balances describe larger scale flows. Geostrophic balances have more effect in the deep
 ocean whereas ekman balances are more prevalent near the surface. Answers may vary.

One point per diagram label, plus one for continental shelf as the diverse marine habitat.

questions.prompt: Authored written substitute for unavailable source material: Distinguish column ozone from surface concentration.
questions.context:
Unit: Climate systems, ozone, cycles, and geohazards.
Worked-case data: A flood map shows 10 km² inundated, but no settlement or infrastructure data are provided. What can be concluded?

criteria.answer: Transmits energy and measures its return.
Light Detection and Ranging; laser/light pulses.
Absorption attenuates reflected radiance, as does scattering out of the line of sight. Accept absorption (published answer) or both.

Three valid thermal-imagery climate measurements, such as sea surface temperature, land surface temperature, cloud temperature/height, or water-vapor information from appropriate thermal absorption bands. The original key allows other reasonable examples.

Historical list with launch dates: OCO-2 July 2, 2014; GCOM-W1 May 18, 2012; Aqua May 4, 2002; CloudSat April 28, 2006; CALIPSO April 28, 2006; Aura July 15, 2004; PARASOL December 18, 2004. PARASOL was no longer in the train in 2017. Assess names and dates together within one practice point.

Historical key order: OCO-2 leads; GCOM-W1 11 minutes behind OCO-2; Aqua 4 minutes behind GCOM-W1; CloudSat 2 minutes 30 seconds behind Aqua; CALIPSO at most 15 seconds behind CloudSat; Aura 15 minutes behind Aqua. Do not substitute a present-day roster.

NASA: National Aeronautics and Space Administration, United States; CSA/ASC: Canadian Space Agency/Agence spatiale canadienne, Canada; CNES: Centre national d’études spatiales/National Centre for Space Studies, France; JAXA: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, Japan. Accept the source’s Japanese Aerospace wording.
Afternoon Train: the satellites cross the equator at about 1:30 pm local solar time.

Sun-synchronous/heliosynchronous orbit: the orbital plane precesses with Earth’s annual motion, maintaining nearly fixed local solar crossing time and similar illumination for repeated observations. Do not require the incorrect claim that the satellite is always in sunlight.

OCO-2 (Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2). Bands approximately 0.765 μm for oxygen A-band, 1.61 μm for weak CO2, 2.06 μm for strong CO2. Three grating spectrometers; f/1.8 near-infrared Cassegrain telescope. The source allows spectrometer. Assess the complete response within one practice point.
CALIPSO: Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP), profiling aerosols and clouds. Its imaging infrared radiometer (IIR) supplies cirrus emissivity and particle-size information.
Methane, CH4 (historical greenhouse-gas context of the source).

The key says ozone. Accept stratospheric ozone depletion with its cooling/negative-forcing explanation; do not claim that increased tropospheric ozone cools the climate. Also accept scattering aerosols such as sulfate with an explanation of negative radiative forcing, since the question does not identify a unique substance.

Give two distinct advantages, one point each. Thermal IR: generally finer resolution, a longer historical record, or less sensitivity to surface roughness. Microwave: ordinary-cloud penetration/better coverage or sensing slightly deeper than the IR skin layer. Microwave retrievals still require corrections for atmospheric and surface effects; neither instrument measures a deep-ocean bulk profile.

Any suitable microwave radiometer used by the service, e.g. TMI, AMSR-E, AMSR2, WindSat or GMI. Strictly these are instruments; accept the instrument names explicitly allowed by the published key or their correctly associated satellite.

Balance intercepted solar power πR² S0 with emitted 4πR² σ T⁴. T=(1366/(4×5.67×10^-8))^(1/4)=278.6 K. Use the stated S0=1366; the auxiliary key’s printed 1376.6 is inconsistent with its correct numerical result. Method credit within one practice point.

T=(1366×(1-0.3)/(4×5.67×10^-8))^(1/4)=254.8 K. This is less accurate relative to 288 K (about 33.2 K low versus 9.4 K low), despite including albedo; it still omits greenhouse warming. Assess calculation and comparison within one practice point.

S0(1-alpha)/4=epsilon sigma T⁴, hence epsilon=1366×0.7/(4×5.67×10^-8×288⁴)=0.6128, rounded 0.61. Increasing epsilon lowers the equilibrium temperature; decreasing epsilon raises it. Here epsilon is an effective emissivity factor, not electrical permittivity. Assess value and explanation within one practice point.
A column integrates ozone vertically; it does not directly specify near-ground concentration.

criteria.answer: Active emits its own energy and detects a return; passive measures naturally emitted/reflected energy. One point per correct distinction.

Radar active, conventional echo sonar active, ordinary camera passive, lidar active, infrared sensor passive, radiometer passive. One each; accept passive sonar if explicitly distinguished from echo sounding.

Quality concerns usefulness/perceived suitability; fidelity concerns faithful reproduction of the original signal or scene. One point each; accept objective definitions of image quality involving resolution, noise and contrast.
Wien law: peak wavelength inversely proportional to absolute temperature.
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (1); specular reflection (1).

CERES (accept Terra/Aqua or Suomi NPP as CERES platforms), measuring Earth outgoing longwave radiative flux/energy budget. Two points for instrument/platform identification and two for purpose; this image alone does not uniquely establish Suomi NPP.
GRACE twin satellites (2), gravity variations used to estimate changes in terrestrial water storage/groundwater mass (2). The map is water-storage change over India, not a surface-wave measurement.

Separate scheduled opportunities from quality-controlled observations.
Reject the three cloud-obscured scenes for surface optical measurement.
Retain one usable scene and report the temporal gap.
Nominal revisit does not imply four usable measurements.
OCO-2 (2), remotely measures CO2 and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence used to study photosynthesis (2). The supplied map is labeled SIF, not a generic map of every greenhouse gas/aerosol.

Warming melts bright ice, exposing darker water/land, lowering albedo and increasing solar absorption, causing further warming and melting: positive feedback. The source key’s decreasing melt rate is incorrect.
Examples: more cloud water, greater optical thickness, or smaller droplets at fixed water content. Credit a valid explanation.

Any correctly explained climate feedback other than ice-albedo, e.g. warming increases water vapor, strengthening greenhouse warming (positive); or warming increases outgoing thermal radiation (negative). Identify direction and causal loop, one point each.
Scattering aerosols such as sulfates generally cool; absorbing black carbon can warm the atmosphere. One point each, allowing cloud-mediated effects with sound reasoning.

Explain two factors, two points each: increased albedo reduces absorbed sunlight and equilibrium temperature; more greenhouse gas increases infrared opacity and surface temperature. Other physically valid atmospheric/surface changes accepted.

Choose two gases and explain natural drivers, two points each. Examples: water vapor responds to evaporation/temperature, CO2 to respiration/photosynthesis/ocean exchange, methane to wetlands. Greenhouse gas and trace gas are overlapping categories, so distinct gases suffice.

A valid climate mitigation or adaptation approach beyond the three Rs, with mechanism. Examples: clean electricity, ecosystem restoration or urban greening reducing heat islands. Full credit for a coherent, scientifically sound explanation.
Resolution resolves small details; contrast distinguishes objects; low noise improves measurement reliability. Credit all three aspects and their contributions; proportional partial credit.
Spectroscopy identifies characteristic absorption/emission features; gas chromatography separates components for identification. Credit scientifically sound techniques and explanations, up to four.
Wien law: 2.898e-3/(5e-7) = 5796 K, approximately 5800 K. Source gives no method credit.
T=9667+273.15=9940.15 K; radiant exitance sigma*T^4 approximately 5.54e8 W/m^2. Credit Kelvin conversion and Stefan-Boltzmann method.

Test Packet

Instructions

6. Ties will be broken by comparing points earned for each question in order.
MIT Invitational - January 24th, 2026 p1 of 8 Remote Sensing C - Test Packet
Section A - 10 points
Suppose you are trying to measure N 2O in the
atmosphere. Image 1 shows some data relating
to N 2O and the general atmosphere.
1. What is the historical chemical name of
N2O? (1)
2. What region of the electromagnetic spec-
trum is shown in Image 1? (1)
3. What type of graph is shown in Image
1? (2)
4. What happens to light at the orange peak
at approximately 4.4 microns in relation to
N2O? (3)
5. Consider the total atmosphere data (pur-
ple) in Image 1. The dominant cause of
atmospheric absorption is a result of which
substance? (2)
6. The absorption in this part of the elec-
tromagnetic spectrum is primarily a result
of what molecular eﬀects in the substance
from the previous question? (1)
Section B - 10 points
Consider a satellite ﬂying eastward in an equa-
torial orbit, which is using Doppler radar to de-
termine its speed relative to the surface.
7. Suppose the satellite sends out radar at a
frequency of 5 GHz and receives a return
signal of 5.0005 GHz. What is the ratio
between the return and outgoing frequen-
cies? (1)
8. What is the speed diﬀerence between the
satellite and the Earth’s surface? Disre-
gard the angular component (altitude ef-
fects) and curvature of the Earth for your
calculations. (4)
9. The Earth has a radius of approximately
6,378 km at the equator. What is the ro-
tational speed of the Earth’s surface at the
equator? (3)
10. What is the orbital speed of this satel-
lite? (2)
Section C - 20 points
Chlorophyll concentration is a particularly im-
portant indicator of the Earth’s current global
productivity. Let’s talk about how it’s mea-
sured.
11. Examine Image 2 , the spectral signature
of chlorophyll-a. Approximately at what
two wavelengths does it absorb blue and red
light, respectively? (2)
12. Image 3 shows spectra from four samples
of seawater with varying concentrations of
chlorophyll. Please explain, in terms of
radiance diﬀerences, why water with high
chlorophyll concentration often appears as
a shade of green rather than blue. (3)
13. Image 4 presents data collected by
PACE displaying chlorophyll concentra-
tions within the ocean over a window in
late 2024. In essence, chlorophyll concen-
trations are another way of measuring the
concentration of what? (1)
14. What is one advantage of PACE’s Sun-
synchronous orbit? (1)
15. Describe why the areas surrounding the
borders of continents have extremely high
chlorophyll concentrations. (2)
16. This image does not display data towards
the north pole; what would data likely look
like in the areas currently not ﬁlled in the
northern hemisphere? Why can data not be
displayed for the entire globe at once? (3)
17. Commonly, collecting chlorophyll-a concen-
trations involves data from the penetration
depth, or z 90. Deﬁne the penetration depth,
or z 90. (2)
18. Some algorithms depend only on surface
chlorophyll-a concentration. In an area
with a well-deﬁned subsurface Chl-a max-
ima layer (SCML), explain why this mea-
surement would be inaccurate. (3)
19. Explain how the location and structure of
the SCML can be accurately modeled. (3)
MIT Invitational - January 24th, 2026 p2 of 8 Remote Sensing C - Test Packet
Section D - 20 points
Refer to Image 5 for these questions. This im-
age shows data collected by CERES, averaged
over many years.
20. Does this image show shortwave or long-
wave radiation? (1)
21. What is the origin of the radiation from Im-
age 5? (2)
22. What property of objects determines the
value of the measurement in Image 5? (2)
23. Consider the light-colored area near the
equator across most of the image, e.g. near
the letter A. What climate phenomenon
causes this area to be light-colored? (2)
24. How does the Earth’s atmospheric circula-
tion produce the phenomenon from the pre-
vious question? (2)
Consider also Image 6 for these questions. This
image also shows data collected by CERES, av-
eraged over many years.
25. Does this image show shortwave or long-
wave radiation? (1)
26. Do the yellow areas on this map indicate
high or low radiation? (1)
27. The blue/purple regions on this map can
be divided into three broad categories cor-
responding to what surface climatological
conditions? (3)
28. What is the reason why each category from
the previous question shows up as blue/pur-
ple on this map? (6)
