criteria.answer: A ripple marks; B mud cracks; C cross bedding; D graded bedding. 1 point each.
A low to moderate; B very low; C moderate to high; D high to decreasing. 1 point each.
B (mud cracks): wet sediment dries and shrinks after exposure to air.
C (cross bedding): inclined layers dip in the sediment-transport direction.

Published rubric: accept any reasonable explanation. A valid explanation relates normal grading (coarser base, finer top as flow wanes) to determining younging direction; overturned beds reverse this orientation.

Published key: A cooling; B melting; C weathering & lithification; D igneous rock; E magma; F melting; G heat & pressure; H weathering & lithification; I sediment; J compaction & cementation; K heat & pressure; L metamorphic rock; M sedimentary rock. For C/H accept the scientifically correct weathering/erosion (these arrows lead to loose sediment). The source assigns 7 points to the complete diagram without per-blank weights; award proportional partial credit.
Weathering and erosion: temperature, precipitation and biological activity control weathering rates and sediment transport. Other defensible processes may receive partial credit.
Any two: no fixed sequence, multiple pathways, steps skipped/repeated, driven by internal Earth and external solar energy.
Any two: little/no subduction; reduced metamorphism/magma production; fewer volcanoes/mountain belts; dominance of surface weathering, erosion and deposition.
Burial: slate. Heating: schist or gneiss. Partial melting: magma, granite or rhyolite. 1 point per stage.
Burial: low-grade metamorphism. Heating: regional metamorphism. Partial melting: melting and crystallization. 1 point per stage.

The published key prints M, R, A, E, Y, P, G, Fa, S, B, W, Fb, T, which runs oldest to youngest in its interpretation. Accept its reverse T, Fb, W, B, S, Fa, G, P, Y, E, A, R, M for the requested youngest-to-oldest order; do not penalize a clearly labeled consistent orientation. Fossils occur in a predictable order, so comparing fossil types shows which layer is older or younger.
Relative dating gives age order; absolute dating gives numerical ages using radiometric methods.
Continental volcanic arcs or hotspots; high silica increases viscosity and traps gas.
Directed pressure during regional metamorphism aligns minerals.
Accumulation and lithification of shell material from marine organisms.
Obduction of mantle material or emplacement in ophiolite complexes.
Preserves graded bedding from turbidity currents, indicating submarine-slope processes and flow direction.

a Bauxite; b Azurite; c Aragonite; d Augite; e Aragonite; f Apatite; g Albite; h Barite; i Barite. One point each.
Mafic composition, rapid cooling near the surface, gas bubbles trapped as vesicles. One point each.

Laccolith: lens/dome-shaped intrusion between layers that uplifts overburden. Batholith: large irregular intrusive body with exposed area above 100 square km. Two points shape and two size comparison.
Rock-cycle positions: top metamorphic rock; right magma; bottom-right igneous rock; bottom-left sediment; left sedimentary rock. One point each.

Joints are fractures/discontinuities without significant shear displacement. Cooling/contraction can generate systematic joints, but they are not restricted to igneous rocks. Credit accurate definition and formation explanation.
Top-left coarse-grained/granite; top-middle porphyritic/granite; right vesicular/pumice; bottom-left fine-grained/rhyolite; bottom-middle glassy/obsidian. One per textural label.
a–f: all calcite. One point per image.
Effervescence/bubbles as carbonate reacts with acid to release CO2.
White streak; perfect rhombohedral cleavage in three directions; Mohs 3; specific gravity about 2.7. One each.
Granite A; shale C; sandstone B, C and E. 1.5 each identification group.
1 Laccolith; 2 Dike; 3 Batholith; 4 Dike; 5 Sill; 6 Volcanic neck; 7 Lopolith. One each.
Diamond; native element family. One each.

Diamonds are generally too old for carbon-14 dating. Long-lived radiogenic isotope systems in suitable inclusions can constrain formation age; explain dating inclusions rather than treating diamond carbon as C14-datable.
Carbon under high pressure and temperature in the mantle, often about 140–190 km deep; kimberlite/lamproite can transport diamonds to the crust.
Carat weight, cut, color, clarity; Gemological Institute of America/GIA. One each.
a Triple point; b Critical point. One each.
It may have been guessed or based on a nondiagnostic feature that will fail on another specimen.

Minerals are naturally occurring inorganic solids with defined composition and ordered crystal structure. Rocks are aggregates of minerals/mineraloids and can include organic material. One point each distinction.
Same chemical composition, different crystal structures; differing pressure/temperature conditions can favor different structures. One each.
1 Contact metamorphism; 2 Volcanic arc; 3 Collisional mountain belt; 4 Stable continent; 5 Accretionary prism. One each.

Increasing grade generally means higher temperature/pressure and more recrystallization or mineral changes. Low grade example slate; high grade example gneiss (or well-qualified schist). Describe each and give examples.
Native; Element; elements. One point each blank.
Silicon and oxygen are abundant in the crust, and linked silica tetrahedra allow many structural arrangements and substitutions. Two points.
Vitreous/pearly luster; density about 2.317 g/cm^3; transparent/translucent; CaSO4·2H2O. One each.
a Discontinuous; b Continuous. One each.
a Ultramafic; b Mafic; c Intermediate; d Felsic. One each.
a Coquina, sedimentary rock; b Silver, native element; c Calcite, carbonate; d Talc, silicate. One point each name/category.
Specimen c / calcite. Birefringence gives two refracted rays with different refractive indices and produces a doubled image. One identification and two explanation points.

Two points per trend: largest atomic radius toward the bottom left (francium in the simplified school trend); highest ionization energy is helium at the top right; highest electron affinity is chlorine among the halogens, not the noble gases; largest molar mass toward the bottom right of the supplied periodic table. Accept verbal locations where appropriate instead of marking the PDF.

Four points per explanation: atomic radius increases down groups as shells are added and generally decreases across a period as effective nuclear charge rises; ionization energy generally rises across a period and upward as electrons are more tightly held, with helium highest; electron affinity reflects the energetics of adding an electron, generally strongest for halogens, with chlorine exceeding fluorine because of fluorine’s compact-shell repulsion and noble gases being unfavorable; molar mass generally increases with increasing proton and neutron count down and across the table, with exceptions. Do not require the source key’s incorrect implication that noble gases have the highest electron affinity.

Oxidation half-reaction: C2H5OH + H2O -> CH3COOH + 4 H+ + 4 e- (1). Reduction: CrO4^2- + 8 H+ + 3 e- -> Cr^3+ + 4 H2O (1). Overall: 4 CrO4^2- + 3 C2H5OH + 20 H+ -> 4 Cr^3+ + 3 CH3COOH + 13 H2O (1).

K2CrO4 is limiting: 2.00/194.20 = 0.0103 mol versus 1.00/46.07 = 0.0217 mol ethanol; ratio chromate:ethanol=4:3 (1). Acetic acid yield=0.0103 x 3/4 = 0.00772 mol, corresponding to 0.464 g CH3COOH (1). Ethanol remaining=1.00 - (2.00/194.20 x 3/4 x 46.07)=0.644 g (1).

The Wheatstone Bridge allows measurement of an unknown resistance to a very high degree of precision. It uses a diamond shape, where one of the sides is an unknown resistance and the rest are known. The resistance can be found by measuring the current flow through the middle of the diamond when the sides are connected.

Resistivity is a material property. It is the inverse of conduction and measures a material’s resistance to the flow of electrons per unit length through a certain cross sectional area. Its units are ohm-meters.

Drift velocity is the overall speed and direction that electrons travel through a material, not including any components of movement perpendicular to the direction of motion. Current (measured in amperes), implicitly uses drift velocity when talked about in terms of the speed of electron flow.

questions.prompt: Authored written substitute for unavailable source material: Solve this case and explain your reasoning: Two point charges keep their values while separation triples. Predict force.

criteria.answer: Full-wave rectification replaces each missing negative half-cycle by its positive reflection: positive humps also on t=1–2 and t=3–4 (1); the original humps, peak 1, zeros at integer times and doubled ripple frequency are retained (1). A precise written waveform description is acceptable instead of drawing.

Electron current is electron flow from negative to positive terminal (1). Drift is slow, typically about 10^-4 to 10^-3 m/s in the key, depending on conductor/current density (1); do not confuse drift speed with field propagation.

Energy flux is energy transfer per unit area per unit time (1); electromagnetic fields carry it around the conductor (1) into the resistive load where work is done (1); units W/m^2 (1); Poynting vector S=E cross H (1).
Thermal energy (1), mechanical/kinetic energy (1), and sound/acoustic energy (1).
The real component of impedance equals resistance: Re(Z)=28.3 ohms. Award two points for the correct value with units. The key labels the question two points but only marks one beside its value.
Use VC/Vmax=1-exp(-t/tau) (1), substitute 0.47 so exp(-t/tau)=0.53 (1), take logs t/tau=-ln(0.53) (1), approximately 0.634 time constants (1).

By symmetry VD=VE=VB (1) and VG=VC=VF (1). Reduce the network to three series groups: three 1-ohm edges in parallel, six 1-ohm edges in parallel, three 1-ohm edges in parallel (3 total for the three groups, including equivalent reasoning). R_AG=1/3+1/6+1/3=5/6 ohm, approximately 0.833 ohm (1). The source question maximum is six; the key’s eight-point method is consolidated to six.

LED arrangement: independently driven parallel branches, each with current limiting (1 point). Working sequence/design (10 points): a valid arrangement yielding Green -> Yellow -> Red -> Green, with 2–3 s per stage and labeled components. One valid design is a 555 astable clock feeding a decade counter, Q0/Q1/Q2 driving individually current-limited green/yellow/red LEDs and Q3 resetting the counter. Explain power/ground and pin connections, reset/enable and clock wiring, LED branches and timing. T=0.693(R1+2R2)C; for example R1=47 kΩ, R2=100 kΩ, C=15 µF gives approximately 2.57 s. The key’s R1=10 kΩ,R2=100 kΩ,C=10 µF gives 1.46 s and does not meet the requested timing. Other demonstrably working circuits receive full credit. The original key explicitly accepts a switch-clocked counter if the operator waits 2–3 s per press; explain that timing procedure. Merely copying a named solution without workable connections/timing is insufficient.

Use F proportional to 1/r².
Replacing r with 3r multiplies the denominator by nine.
The new magnitude is F/9; attraction or repulsion is unchanged.
Direction depends on signs, not distance alone.

Three days ago, fifty-two high students from around the world arrived at Yale, for the Yale Young
Global Scholars program. Some of them, however, had other aims...

crime took place from 10:47 PM to 10:49 PM. Due to the late hour, no witnesses were to be seen,

carved into it. Despite the video's bad quality, Yale Police have narrowed down the search to four
students, who were late for the 11 PM lights out attendance at the Omni New Haven Hotel. The
Omni Hotel is a 5-minute walk from old campus. The Police now need your help to investigate and
discover the mischief maker.
TheSuspects
All four suspects were wearing different colored clothes the night of the crime, however their
friends do not recall the specific colors of their outfits. Black overalls were found in Jake and Chris's
luggage; however, the low video quality might be inconclusive evidence.
Jake is medium sized, and is a known mischief-maker at school. He is a smoker, and was caught
with a packet of cigarettes on Yale's campus, on the day of the crime. He was absent from the
workshop throughout the day, only attending it for the first twenty minutes or so. He returned
to his room at 11:o2 PM, and said he was hanging out with some Yale undergraduates. The
police have failed to confirm his story.
Chris is a tall fair guy, and wears glasses. He owns a German Shephard, and had brought the
dog on campus for the event. He is a chocoholic, and is known to carry his stash with him,
wherever he goes. His whereabouts were unknown from around 1o:oo PM to 11:1o PM.
Dave is a tall guy, who is a famous athlete at Westminster school. He is extremely organized,
and carries around a planner and pen with himself all the time. He left his room for a bathroom
break at around 1o:45 PM and returned twenty minutes later. His teachers consider him least
likely to have committed the vandalism, since he is ‘not that kind of a kid’ to quote
Westminster's staff advisor.
Andreas is short, and is normally well-behaved, according to his teachers. However, he has a
short temper and often resorts to destruction when teased by his peers. He has a serious
demeanor, and normally remains to the point. He left the hotel for half an hour, at around
10:30 PM, saying he was going out to get some fresh air.
The Yale Police will provide you with four updates as their investigation continues.
Section I - Short Questions
[5o points]
1) A white powder was found at the scene of the crime. It burns to give an orange flame. What
might the powder be? [2 points]
a. calcium chloride
c. lithium chloride
b. calcium carbonate
d. magnesium sulfate
2) Traces of a white powder were also found in Jake's pocket. When some dilute ethanoic acid was
poured onto it, a gas was produced which turned lime water milky.
a)What is the gas? [2 points]
b) What might the white powder be? [2 points]
a. lithium chloride
c. sodium chloride
b. sodium carbonate
d. calcium nitrate
YUSO 2017 FORENSICS EXAMINATION
3) What would you use to identify cornstarch? [2 points]
a. cobalt
c. Iodine
b. ethanol
d. ammonia
Update 1: A plastic wrap containing traces of beef jerky was found at a garbage can beside the statue.
4) A faint odor of burnt hair can be noticed from the plastic.
What is the plastic? [2 points]
a.PVC
c.PTFE
b.LDPE
d.HDPE
Update 2: The Yale Police has now decided to use DNA analysis. You will be provided with the results soon.
5) What type of bonds do guanine-cytosine and adenine-thymine form? [2 points]
6) The DNA fingerprints taken from blood samples of Andreas, Chris, Dave and Jake respectively,

Does the crime scene sample match the DNA fingerprints of any of the subjects? If yes, to whom
does the evidence point? Explain. [2 points]
A

It does not identify one of these suspects. The public statue may have unrelated deposited DNA; a mismatch can still inform exclusion of a particular profile, so accept a justified discussion of its limitations/usefulness.
Outer cuticle; cortex beneath; central medulla; root at base. One point per correctly located label.

Discuss denser/coarser dog coat versus the human comparison, often larger/continuous animal medulla versus thinner/fragmented human medulla, and more synchronized/seasonal coat growth versus more asynchronous human scalp-hair growth. Allow species, hair type and growth-cycle qualifications; neither grows indefinitely.
Human is the published interpretation; explain relatively distributed pigmentation and the pictured shaft features. Microscopy supports classification, not individual identification.
None specifically; all suspects are human.

Spot sample and standards on a pencil baseline above solvent; place paper in solvent chamber; let solvent rise and separate components; mark solvent front and compare component travel/Rf. One point per major step, maximum four.
Compare the unknown ink separation/Rf pattern to suspect inks; a matching pattern supports a common ink but is not unique proof of guilt.
Jake: ink spots have the same relative positions/Rf pattern as the crime-scene sample. Award identification plus explanation.
Jake; the concentric/whorl ridge pattern matches the class shown. Explain the pattern; class similarity alone is not individual identification.

Iodine vapor adsorbs to fingerprint residues and produces transient brown prints on suitable porous material. Describe an enclosed chamber and controlled vapor exposure under fume extraction, observation and prompt photography/fixation, suitable porous surfaces, and fading/limited durability. Six relevant rubric elements, one each; this is a written procedure question.
Splash goggles, suitable gloves, protective clothing and use of a fume hood/avoid inhalation. One point each valid distinct precaution.

criteria.answer: 1 point each: influenza is an RNA virus with error-prone RNA polymerase; mutations occur frequently; circulating strains therefore change; the vaccine is updated to match the new strains.

1 point each: His274 is replaced by Tyr274; drug binding normally moves Glu276 toward His274; the bulkier Tyr pushes Glu276 back into the active site; this reduces drug binding space/affinity so the drug is displaced while substrate binding can continue.

1 point each: lower endosomal pH; triggers conformational change; exposes the buried hydrophobic fusion peptide so it inserts into the membrane; enables membrane fusion and transfer of viral genetic material.

0.5 point: shift abruptly creates new subtypes. 1 point: animal transmission or reassortment/mixing contributes to shift. 0.5 point: drift gradually changes HA/NA antigens. 0.5 point: point mutations cause drift. 0.5 point: mutations can alter the HA binding pocket without losing overall function. 1 point: altered antigens escape existing antibodies, allowing illness.
1 point each: vaccines induce antibodies; prime protective immunity before infection; antivirals block a viral protein needed for replication; therefore limit replication in an existing infection.
